title: Windows auto-update ships with code-signature verification disabled (verifyUpdateCodeSignature=false) on unsigned builds
evidence: Release workflow, Windows branch: `echo "::warning::No AZURE_CLIENT_ID — publishing an UNSIGNED Windows build (SmartScreen warns; update signature check disabled)."` then `pnpm exec electron-builder --publish always $VER_FLAG --config.win.verifyUpdateCodeSignature=false`. electron-builder bakes this into app-update.yml, so the SHIPPED client skips electron-updater's Authenticode check (NsisUpdater.verifySignature → _verifyUpdateCodeSignature). The shell auto-downloads + auto-installs on quit unconditionally for packaged builds: main.ts:382-383 `autoUpdater.autoDownload = true; autoUpdater.autoInstallOnAppQuit = true;` and main.ts:399-401 checks on launch + every 6h. sha512 from latest.yml is still verified (mitigates a pure network MITM since latest.yml is HTTPS-from-GitHub), but the publisher-identity gate is gone.
impact: If the GitHub Releases channel is compromised (leaked GITHUB_TOKEN, a malicious release author, or anyone with write to CyberSystema/libriant Releases), an attacker can publish a release with a matching latest.yml + sha512 and every Windows client silently downloads and installs an arbitrary, unsigned executable on next quit — fleet-wide remote code execution on librarian desktops. The Authenticode layer that would normally stop a swapped binary is explicitly off. Ships this way today because the Azure signing secrets are not yet configured.
fix: Sign Windows builds (Azure Trusted Signing secrets) before any production rollout so verifyUpdateCodeSignature stays at its secure default. If shipping unsigned is unavoidable interim, DISABLE auto-update on the unsigned Windows path (don't call autoUpdater for unsigned builds) rather than disabling the signature check — an unsigned auto-updater is the worst of both worlds. Also restrict who can publish GitHub Releases and protect the release tag.

adversarial.reason: Independently confirmed; the claim is accurate and not overstated. CODE FACTS (all verified): (1) .github/workflows/desktop-release.yml Windows leg, unsigned branch runs `pnpm exec electron-builder --publish always $VER_FLAG --config.win.verifyUpdateCodeSignature=false` with the warning "update signature check disabled" — this is the DEFAULT shipping path today because the AZURE_* secrets are not configured (SIGNING.md "ship now, sign later"; apps/desktop/electron-builder.yml:72-81 win section documents the same). electron-builder writes verifyUpdateCodeSignature into the packaged app-update.yml, so the shipped NsisUpdater skips electron-updater's Authenticode/publisher-identity check. (2) The client auto-updates unconditionally for packaged builds: apps/desktop/src/main.ts:382-383 `autoUpdater.autoDownload = true; autoUpdater.autoInstallOnAppQuit = true;`, checks on launch and every 6h (main.ts:399-401), and initAutoUpdate() IS actually invoked (main.ts:484; quitAndInstall at main.ts:433). IMPACT: if the GitHub Releases channel is compromised (leaked GITHUB_TOKEN, malicious release author, or anyone with write to Releases), an attacker publishes a release whose latest.yml lists the sha512 of their own malicious unsigned binary; every Windows client then silently downloads and installs it on next quit — fleet-wide RCE on librarian desktops. The Authenticode layer that would normally reject a binary not signed by the legitimate publisher is explicitly off. ADVERSARIAL CHECKS: No existing guard prevents this — unlike macOS, where unsigned => auto-update is fully DISABLED (a safe posture), the Windows path leaves auto-update ENABLED with verification DISABLED (the "worst of both worlds" the fix calls out). The sha512-from-latest.yml check the report itself credits as a mitigation only stops a pure network MITM (latest.yml is HTTPS from GitHub); it does NOT help in the Releases-compromise scenario because the attacker controls latest.yml. Severity HIGH not CRITICAL is correct per the rubric: exploitation requires a precondition (Releases-channel/supply-chain compromise) and there is no unauthenticated network path to RCE against the default-secure feed, so it is an ops/DR + supply-chain risk rather than a directly exploitable bug on the running product. Cited files/lines are accurate; nothing misread or overstated.

title: No CPU/memory limits on any container in the single-host prod stack — one OOM/runaway takes down Postgres and the entire cell
evidence: `grep -n 'deploy:|resources:|limits:|mem_limit|cpus|memory:' docker-compose.prod.yml` returns nothing (exit 1). All seven services (caddy, migrate, api, web, worker, postgres, pgbouncer, redis) share the host with no containment; only `worker` has `stop_grace_period: 60s`. The compose header (lines 3-14) states this is a single host with app + data tiers co-located, and the alert rules anticipate the failure mode — HostLowMemory/HostSwapping/HostHighCPU (infra/monitoring/alerts.yml:30-72) — but nothing bounds a container. A bulk import, a runaway report query, or an api/worker memory leak can exhaust host RAM; the kernel OOM-killer or thrashing can take Postgres (the same box) with it.
impact: A single tenant's heavy workload or one leaking process is a whole-cell availability and potential data-integrity risk (Postgres killed mid-write). On the documented single-host topology there is no blast-radius containment between the noisy workload and the database.
fix: Add `deploy.resources.limits` (memory + cpus) and `mem_reservation` to at least api, web, worker (cap each well under host RAM), and a memory reservation/limit guardrail for postgres + redis. With plain `docker compose up` (not Swarm) use the `mem_limit`/`cpus`/`pids_limit` top-level keys, which compose honours. Also set Postgres `shared_buffers`/`work_mem` consistent with the chosen limit.

adversarial.reason: CONFIRMED. I independently verified infra/compose/docker-compose.prod.yml: no `deploy.resources`, `mem_limit`, `cpus`, `mem_reservation`, or `pids_limit` on ANY of the 7 services (caddy, migrate, api, web, worker, postgres, pgbouncer, redis). My grep for `deploy:|resources:|limits:|mem_limit|cpus|memory:|reservations|pids_limit` across infra/compose/ returned nothing (exit 1), matching the claim. Topology is confirmed single-host: the compose header (lines 1-22) and docs/deployment-hetzner.md describe one Hetzner box where Postgres shares the host with api/web/worker on private networks; deployment is plain `docker compose up` (NOT Swarm — confirmed via the guide and `restart: unless-stopped` usage), and `infra/deploy/fleet.yml` is just a host list with no resource config and no override compose file applies limits. Postgres is set only with `max_connections=200` and `shared_preload_libraries` — no `shared_buffers`/`work_mem` bound (docker-compose.prod.yml:275-283). The alert rules independently corroborate the anticipated failure mode: HostLowMemory (<12% RAM), HostSwapping (>50%), HostHighCPU (>85%, description literally says "Check for a bulk import/report") at infra/monitoring/alerts.yml:30-72, and the documented remediation is "grow the box" (Part 15) with only a 2G swapfile as cushion (deployment-hetzner.md:189-192) — i.e., no per-container blast-radius containment. The precondition (bulk import, runaway report, or an api/worker leak) is reachable in ordinary multi-tenant usage, so a noisy workload can drive the host OOM-killer/thrashing and take down co-located Postgres. I could NOT find any guard refuting this (no daemon ulimits, no systemd cgroup limits, no swarm deploy block). Notably Redis sets `--maxmemory-policy allkeys-lru` but no `--maxmemory`, so even that policy is inert — further confirming the gap. SEVERITY: correctly HIGH per the rubric (ops/DR with a reachable precondition), NOT critical: an OOM-kill of Postgres is crash-consistent (WAL+fsync) and recovers, so the claim's "potential data-integrity risk / Postgres killed mid-write" framing is overstated — this is a single-host availability/DR issue, not exploitable data corruption. With that one caveat trimmed, the finding is real, accurately evidenced (the author did not misread), and appropriately rated high.

title: multer 2.1.1 (direct prod dep) — two DoS advisories reachable via 5 live authenticated upload endpoints
evidence: apps/api/package.json:24 declares "multer": "^2.1.1"; installed = 2.1.1 (node_modules/.pnpm/multer@2.1.1). `pnpm why multer -r` shows it as a production dependency of @libriant/api both directly and via @nestjs/platform-express (which pins multer 2.1.1 as a hard dep, peer:none). Two advisories apply: GHSA-72gw-mp4g-v24j (high — DoS via deeply nested field names, <2.2.0) and GHSA-3p4h-7m6x-2hcm (moderate — DoS via incomplete cleanup of aborted uploads, <2.2.0). Reachable: FileInterceptor is wired into live endpoints — import.controller.ts:70 `@UseInterceptors(FileInterceptor('file', { limits: { fileSize: IMPORT_MAX_UPLOAD_BYTES } }))` with `@Body() body: Record<string,string>` (multipart text fields parsed); plus covers.controller.ts:39, photos.controller.ts:39, branding.controller.ts:55, storage-demo.controller.ts:83. The deeply-nested-field-name parse happens in multer before route validation, so the fileSize limit does not prevent it.
impact: An authenticated tenant user (endpoints sit behind TenantGuard; import also RolesGuard/PlanGuard) can send a multipart request with deeply nested field names or repeatedly abort uploads to exhaust CPU/memory/disk on the shared API worker, degrading the service for all tenants. This is a same-major minor bump compatible with @nestjs/platform-express@11's hard dep on 2.1.1 (the override supersedes it). title: Sensitive admin & billing mutations write no audit_log row (revenue/entitlement changes are untraceable)
evidence: The control-plane AuditEvent model (packages/db-control/prisma/schema.prisma:878, @@map("audit_log")) exists precisely for this — it has actorType/actorId/action/beforeJson/afterJson/ip/userAgent and even documents `subscription.changed` as an example action (line 884). But `auditEvent.create` is called in only 3 places (admin-tenants.controller.ts:204 tenant hard-delete, tenant-audit.service.ts:48, platform-settings/admin-subscriptions.controller.ts:42). billing.service.ts:379-380 comments `audit happen exactly once per state change`, yet applyAdminPlanChange() (l.388) and applyManualPayment() (l.410) just do `controlDb.subscription.update(...)` with NO audit write. Confirmed via grep: admin-overrides, admin-plans, and admin-system-mode controllers contain zero `auditEvent`/`audit`/`logger.` references. So a Libriant operator (or a compromised admin session) can grant a tenant a free paid plan, extend paidUntil indefinitely, flip platform-wide pricing, toggle feature overrides, or trigger a global maintenance/out_of_order takeover with no durable, queryable record of who/when/before/after.
impact: No forensic trail for revenue-affecting and platform-wide control actions performed by staff. Defeats insider-abuse detection, fraud investigation (manual paid-until grants), incident reconstruction (who took the fleet down), and any SOC2/GDPR accountability claim. Use actions like subscription.changed, subscription.paid_until_set, plan.updated, feature_override.set, system_mode.set. The schema is already there; only the writes are missing.

title: ReDoS guard bypassed by bounded {n} repetition of an ambiguous group — platform-wide event-loop freeze
evidence: hasAmbiguousRepeatedGroup only treats a group as 'repeated' when followed by * , + , or an OPEN-ENDED brace: `const repeated = next === '*' || next === '+' || (next === '{' && isOpenEndedBrace(p, i + 1));` and isOpenEndedBrace requires a comma: `return /^\{\d*,\d*\}/.test(p.slice(at));` (field-types.ts:134-135). So a fixed-count brace `{n}` is NOT considered repetition, and a nested-quantifier group repeated a fixed number of times slips past. patternLooksCatastrophic's other gates don't catch it either (length<200, no stacked quantifiers, countUnbounded<=6). Empirically verified against the exact guard code reimplemented from this file: pattern `(a*){5}c` PASSES the guard and `re.test('a'.repeat(40)+'!')` took 319ms; `([a-z]*){8}$` PASSES and never finished within 12s on a 35-char input (exponential). Probe output: `PASSES (a*){5}c  50:1047.0ms  100:10272.8ms ABORT(>4s)` and `PASSES ([a-z]*){8}$  50:64243.2ms ABORT(>4s)`.
impact: An owner/admin saves a malicious validation pattern (e.g. `([a-z]*){8}$`) on any built-in custom field (book/member/loan/reservation/book_copy) or collection field — patternSaveError accepts it on all four write paths. Thereafter ANY user who creates/updates such a record and supplies a ~40-char value for that field reaches validateField (field-types.ts:323-334), which re-screens with the SAME bypassed patternLooksCatastrophic (returns false), passes the REGEX_INPUT_CAP=2000 length check, then runs re.test(raw) and freezes the single Node event loop for tens of seconds — a denial of service for EVERY tenant on that API process, per request. The bulk import path (import-engine.ts:164 → validateRecord) runs the same pattern once per row, amplifying the freeze across an entire import. The input cap does not help because blowup is exponential and triggers far below 2000 chars. The code comments (field-types.ts:38-40,55-61,228-229) explicitly claim the exponential class is rejected and only polynomial residual remains — that claim is false.
fix: Treat ANY repetition quantifier after a group — including bounded `{n}` and `{n,m}` — as 'repeated' when screening bodyIsAmbiguous: change isOpenEndedBrace to also match exact `{n}` (n>=2) and bounded `{n,m}`, i.e. flag `(ambiguousBody){k}` for k>=2. Also flag a nested unbounded quantifier inside a fixed-repeat group. Add the bypass cases (`(a*){5}c`, `([a-z]*){8}$`, `(a|a){10}`, `(.*){10}`) to redos-guard.spec.ts as must-reject. Strongly recommended: move custom-field regex matching off the main event loop or onto a non-backtracking engine (RE2 / recheck), since heuristic scanners will keep missing shapes; at minimum run validateField's regex with a hard per-call time budget (worker thread / vm timeout).

adversarial.reason: Independently confirmed. The guard treats a group as repeated only for *, +, or an OPEN-ENDED brace: hasAmbiguousRepeatedGroup at field-types.ts:126 uses `next === '{' && isOpenEndedBrace(p, i + 1)`, and isOpenEndedBrace at field-types.ts:134-135 is `/^\{\d*,\d*\}/.test(p.slice(at))` which REQUIRES a comma. So a fixed-count brace `(...){n}` (no comma) is never treated as repetition, and its body is never screened by bodyIsAmbiguous. I reimplemented the exact guard from this file: `(a*){5}c`, `([a-z]*){8}$`, `(a|a){10}`, `(.*){10}` all return false (PASS), while open-ended `(a+)+`/`(.*)*` are correctly rejected. The other gates do not catch it: length<200, no stacked `[*+][*+]`, and countUnbounded for `([a-z]*){8}$` is 1 (<=6). Runtime is genuinely exponential and triggers far below REGEX_INPUT_CAP=2000: in fresh node processes `([a-z]*){8}$` on inputs of 23/26/29/32/35 chars took ~1s/2.5s/5.8s/12s/24s (each +3 chars ~doubles), so a single ~35-char value freezes the shared event loop ~24s. title: RESEND_API_KEY never reaches the containers — documented EMAIL_DRIVER=resend path crash-loops the api + worker at boot
evidence: env.ts reads it: `resendApiKey: process.env.RESEND_API_KEY?.length ? process.env.RESEND_API_KEY : null` (env.ts:360), and the Resend driver hard-fails without it: `if (!env.resendApiKey) { throw new Error('EMAIL_DRIVER=resend requires RESEND_API_KEY (re_...).'); }` (apps/api/src/email/drivers/resend-driver.ts:31-33). The prod compose x-app-env block injects SMTP_URL/EMAIL_FROM/EMAIL_DRIVER but NOT RESEND_API_KEY — `grep -rn RESEND infra/` returns nothing. The block's own comment warns this is load-bearing: 'every driver var the app reads MUST be listed here — Compose only injects variables referenced in this block, not everything in .env.prod' (compose lines 56-57). Deploy sources the file (`set -a; . /srv/libriant/.env.prod; set +a`, deploy.yml) so RESEND_API_KEY is in the host shell, but Compose drops any var it doesn't reference. The worker builds the same driver: `const driver = createEmailDriver()` (apps/api/src/email/email-worker.ts:64) and inherits `<<: *app-env` (compose:239).
impact: An operator who follows .env.prod.example (lines 77-78 document RESEND_API_KEY for EMAIL_DRIVER=resend) and sets EMAIL_DRIVER=resend + RESEND_API_KEY in /srv/libriant/.env.prod gets resendApiKey=null inside the container; both the api and the email worker throw at construction and crash-loop. Fail-closed (no silent insecure send), but it breaks a first-class, documented production email backend and would manifest as a failed deploy with a misleading 'requires RESEND_API_KEY' error even though the operator DID set it.
fix: Add `RESEND_API_KEY: ${RESEND_API_KEY:-}` to the x-app-env block in infra/compose/docker-compose.prod.yml (next to SMTP_URL) so it propagates to both api and worker; mirror it in .env.prod.example management if needed.

adversarial.reason: Independently confirmed across the full chain. (1) RESEND_API_KEY is documented in .env.prod.example as the var to set for EMAIL_DRIVER=resend (lines 72 "EMAIL_DRIVER=resend + RESEND_API_KEY=re_..." and 78 "RESEND_API_KEY="). title: STRIPE-RETRY-STALE-REPLAY gap: subscription.deleted has no id/monotonic guard — a replayed stale delete clobbers a newer re-subscription
file: apps/api/src/billing/billing.service.ts:599-625 (handleStripeSubscriptionDeleted); guard exists only at :549-560 in syncStripeSubscription; sweep at apps/api/src/jobs/stripe-retry.job.ts:52-60,132-134
evidence: handleStripeSubscriptionDeleted resolves the tenant by customer id only — `const billing = await controlDb.billingAccount.findFirst({ where: { stripeCustomerId: payload.customer } })` — then UNCONDITIONALLY downgrades: `controlDb.subscription.update({ where:{tenantId}, data:{ planId: starter.id, status:'canceled', stripeSubscriptionId:null, currentPeriodStart:null, ... } })`. It never checks that `payload.id` matches the currently-stored `existing.stripeSubscriptionId`. By contrast syncStripeSubscription guards out-of-order events: `if (existing?.stripeSubscriptionId === payload.id && existing.currentPeriodStart != null && nextPeriodStart != null && nextPeriodStart.getTime() < existing.currentPeriodStart.getTime()) { ...return; }`. The retry sweep re-dispatches any row with `processedAt:null` AND (`error not null` OR stale `receivedAt`), and its dispatch() routes customer.subscription.deleted straight back into handleStripeSubscriptionDeleted with the original payloadJson — bypassing the controller's 30-day Redis dedup (the sweep uses its own private lock).
impact: Data-integrity / wrongful loss of paid access. Scenario: tenant cancels sub_A → Stripe sends customer.subscription.deleted(sub_A) which transiently errors (DB blip) and is persisted with error set; the tenant then re-subscribes → customer.subscription.created(sub_B) processes and the tenant is active+paid on sub_B; the stripe-webhook-retry sweep later replays the errored delete event for sub_A, and because there is no id check it downgrades the tenant to Starter/canceled, nulls stripeSubscriptionId/period, and (for paid plans) revokes desktop access and paid features even though Stripe considers sub_B fully active. Self-heals only on the next live subscription.* event for sub_B, leaving a window of wrongful denial and a desync between Stripe and local state.
fix: Add the same monotonic/id guard to handleStripeSubscriptionDeleted: read the existing subscription row and bail (log + return) when `existing.stripeSubscriptionId` is set and does NOT equal `payload.id` (the delete is for a stale/superseded subscription). Only downgrade when the deleted id is the one we currently track (or when we track none).

title: Account-lockout DoS: login lockout is account-wide and renewable, not IP-scoped

The per-IP login budget is RL.loginPerIp = { limit: 20, windowSec: 300 } (auth.controller.ts:55), i.e. a single IP can submit 20 attempts / 5 min — comfortably more than the 5 needed to lock an account. There is no IP-scoping, progressive backoff, or CAPTCHA, so an attacker who knows (slug, email) can keep any account — including the owner — perpetually locked by sending 5 bad passwords every 15 minutes.

title: Service worker caches member-photo/logo PII into STATIC_CACHE, which is never wiped on logout
