impact: If the trusted web app is ever XSS'd (or an http instance is injected), the attacker can call setServerUrl('https://attacker') to make their own server permanently 'trusted' by the shell, gaining persistent access to the privileged bridge (local printer enumeration + silent printing, external-URL opening) across restarts since serverUrl is persisted. Self-perpetuating persistence/pivot; requires an initial foothold so it's an escalation aid rather than a standalone breach.
fix: Gate setServerUrl so it is reachable ONLY from the file:// fallback page (the legitimate reconfiguration surface), not from the live app top frame; e.g. in the handler require frame.url.startsWith('file://') for the mutating set, and treat the live app origin as read-only. Consider an allowlist/confirmation for new origins.

title: ensure-env.sh writes EMAIL_DRIVER=console into .env.prod, which env.ts accepts in production — re-opens the REL-06 reset-token/PII-in-Docker-logs exposure the compose default was written to close
evidence: docker-compose.prod.yml:74 deliberately passes `EMAIL_DRIVER: ${EMAIL_DRIVER:-}` (empty when unset) with a comment (66-73) stating console 'writes password-reset token URLs (account-takeover material) and member PII into retained Docker logs' and that pass-through-empty forces env.ts to fail fast. But the deploy runs `bash scripts/ensure-env.sh --auto` (deploy.yml:259) which executes `ensure_default EMAIL_DRIVER console` (ensure-env.sh:98), writing `EMAIL_DRIVER=console` into /srv/libriant/.env.prod; the deploy then sources that file (deploy.yml:260) so compose's `${EMAIL_DRIVER:-}` resolves to `console`. env.ts then returns it verbatim with no prod guard: `if (raw === 'console' || raw === 'smtp' || raw === 'resend') return raw;` (env.ts:352). console-driver.ts:19-21 logs `to:`, `subj:` and the first 6 body lines at info level — reset/verification links sit at the top of those bodies — into json-file logs retained at 50m×5 (compose:90-95).
impact: Once any real member exists, password-reset and email-verification token URLs plus member PII are written to host Docker logs readable by anyone with host/log access — account-takeover material. The compose comment's claim that the gap is closed is contradicted by ensure-env.sh. (Per project memory this console-only posture is intentional while no email provider is wired, so impact is currently bounded to the closed trial.)
fix: Either stop defaulting EMAIL_DRIVER in ensure-env.sh (leave it unset so compose's pass-through-empty + env.ts fail-fast actually engages), or make env.ts refuse `console` when NODE_ENV=production unless an explicit ALLOW_CONSOLE_EMAIL escape hatch is set. Until a provider is wired, accept the risk explicitly and align the compose comment with reality.

title: Stripe webhook payloads (customer PII) stored unredacted and shipped in control-plane exports
evidence: stripe-webhook.controller.ts:79 persists the FULL event: `payloadJson: event as never` into stripe_webhook_events.payloadJson (schema.prisma:654 `payloadJson Json`, retained ~30d). For invoice.payment_* and customer.subscription.* events the raw Stripe body contains customer PII — customer_email, customer_name, customer_address/billing_details, and card brand/last4. The control-plane export redactor (export-processors.ts redactRow → isSensitive, l.61-66) only matches column NAMES against /token|secret|passwordhash|password_hash/ or the explicit SENSITIVE_COLUMNS map (l.52-57). The column `payloadjson` matches none of these, so readTables (l.390) emits it verbatim. A control/all-scope CSV/JSON/XLSX export therefore writes customer emails, names and billing addresses into an unencrypted file retained 24h on the shared storage volume.
impact: Customer PII at rest in webhook table and exfiltrated into unencrypted export artifacts. GDPR data-minimisation / right-to-erasure exposure and a juicy target if the storage volume or an export download link leaks. Exports are admin-only (mitigating), but the file persists outside auth and the PII is broader than needed for replay.
fix: Either (a) store a slimmed payload (drop customer email/name/address/payment-method details, keep ids + amounts needed for replay), or (b) add `stripe_webhook_events: new Set(['payloadjson'])` to SENSITIVE_COLUMNS so control-plane exports redact it. Also add stripe_webhook_events.error if it can ever carry PII. Set/verify a TTL prune job actually runs (schema says 30d).

title: "volunteer" role (explicitly "limited rights") can create/edit/archive all core data — catalog, members, loans, reservations, copies, custom records — no @Roles gate
evidence: BooksController is `@Controller('t/:slug/catalog/books') @UseGuards(TenantGuard)` with NO @Roles on `@Post()/@Patch(':id')/@Delete(':id')`, and the handlers pass only `tenant` to the service — role is never read. The UserRole enum (packages/db-control/prisma/schema.prisma:41-46) defines `volunteer // limited rights` as the lowest role, and TenantGuard only proves membership, not role. By contrast staff/settings/branding/import/audit/collections-definitions ARE `@Roles('owner','admin')`-gated, and storage-demo.controller.ts:251 explicitly floors sensitive-file reads above `volunteer` (`if (!user || user.role === 'volunteer') throw ForbiddenException`). So a volunteer who is blocked from viewing a member's photo file can still PATCH/DELETE that member record, edit/delete any book, and check out/return/mark-lost loans.
impact: A library account intended as 'limited rights' (e.g. a temporary helper) can destructively mutate the entire catalog, member roster, and circulation ledger. Not a cross-tenant breach (db-per-tenant isolates it) and requires an admin to have created the volunteer account, but it contradicts the documented role semantics and the privacy floor the same codebase applies to member files.
fix: Decide the intended volunteer capability explicitly. If volunteers should only do circulation, add `@UseGuards(RolesGuard) @Roles('owner','admin','librarian')` to the destructive catalog/members routes (POST/PATCH/DELETE) and keep loans open; if the data routes are genuinely meant for all roles, document that and reconcile it with the TEN-06 volunteer file floor so the model is consistent. At minimum gate DELETE/archive and member status changes above volunteer.

title: Cookie Secure / __Host- prefix fails open on any NODE_ENV that is not exactly 'production' (e.g. staging)
evidence: `const cookieSecure = optional('SESSION_COOKIE_SECURE', 'auto'); const isSecure = cookieSecure === 'auto' ? (nodeEnv === 'production' || optional('PUBLIC_APP_URL','http://localhost:3000').startsWith('https://')) : cookieSecure === 'true';`. The forced-Secure leg checks `nodeEnv === 'production'` EXACTLY. Secret-requirement logic elsewhere uses the safer `isDev = nodeEnv === 'development'` (anything non-dev is treated as prod), but the cookie leg does not. isSecure flows into Secure flag AND the __Host- prefix for all three cookies: cookie.service.ts:18/31, admin-cookie.service.ts:19/25, impersonation-cookie.service.ts:13/19, and the cookie-name defaults at env.ts:272-301 (`isSecure ? '__Host-libriant_session' : 'libriant_session'`).
impact: A deploy with NODE_ENV=staging (a common value) that leaves SESSION_COOKIE_SECURE unset/'auto' and PUBLIC_APP_URL on the http default resolves isSecure=false, sending session/admin/impersonation bearer cookies WITHOUT Secure and without the __Host- prefix — they can leak over a plaintext/mixed request. The shipped prod compose hardcodes NODE_ENV=production AND SESSION_COOKIE_SECURE='true', so the official deploy path is safe; the exposure is for any non-compose / staging deploy that relies on the 'auto' default.
fix: Treat all non-development environments as Secure-by-default: change the auto leg to `nodeEnv !== 'development' || PUBLIC_APP_URL.startsWith('https://')`, matching the isDev convention already used for secret enforcement.

title: Effective-plan cache TTL not clamped to graceUntil / paidUntil — lapsed grace or manual paid-until over-grants paid features for up to the full cache TTL
evidence: The resolver SQL correctly drops access at the boundary: `OR (s.status='past_due' AND s."graceUntil" IS NOT NULL AND s."graceUntil" > NOW())` and `AND (s."billingMode" <> 'manual' OR s."paidUntil" IS NULL OR s."paidUntil" > NOW())`. But the cached blob is held for the full TTL: writeCache clamps TTL ONLY to override expiry — `if (soonestOverrideExpiry) { const secsUntilExpiry = ...; ttl = Math.max(1, Math.min(ttl, secsUntilExpiry)); }`. graceUntil, paidUntil and currentPeriodEnd never constrain the TTL. The PQF-3 comment itself admits the failure mode for the analogous override case ("nothing writes a row at the expiry instant"), and there is no scheduled job that invalidates the plan cache when grace/paidUntil lapses (registry.ts has no grace/paidUntil sweep). Default TENANT_CACHE_TTL_SEC is 300.
impact: A past_due tenant whose graceUntil expires mid-cache, or a manual-billed tenant whose paidUntil expires mid-cache, keeps full paid-plan features (and passes plan/quota gates) for up to ~5 minutes (the cache TTL) past the moment access should have dropped. Bounded over-grant, not unbounded, and only on the read path — but it is the same bug class PQF-3 explicitly fixed for overrides, left unfixed for the billing boundaries that matter most.
fix: Extend the TTL-clamp in loadFromDb/writeCache to also consider the soonest of graceUntil (for past_due rows) and paidUntil (for manual rows) — return them alongside soonestOverrideExpiry and clamp the cache EX to the minimum of all upcoming expiries, mirroring the existing override clamp.

title: Offline queue has no entry age-limit but server idempotency results expire after 24h, opening a double-apply window (renew re-extends + re-increments)
evidence: offline-queue stores entries keyed by id with `createdAt` used ONLY for sort (`.sort((a,b)=>a.createdAt-b.createdAt)`); there is no age-based pruning and MAX_REPLAY_ATTEMPTS=6 counts only 5xx, not staleness. The server's idempotency record lives for `RESULT_TTL_SEC = 24*60*60`. Comment in offline-queue.ts claims safety 'rests on idempotency keys ... even if the original request had actually reached the server before the connection dropped' — but that guarantee evaporates once the 24h Redis record expires. Sequence: original POST commits server-side, response is lost on a dropped connection, device stays offline >24h; on reconnect OfflineQueueProvider.flush re-POSTs with the same Idempotency-Key, the interceptor's SETNX now succeeds (idem:<tenant>:<method>:<path>:<key> is gone), and `next.handle()` re-runs the operation. For renew this is a clean double-apply: LoansService.renew re-reads the (still-active) loan and its CAS `updateMany({ where: { id, status:'active', renewedCount: loan.renewedCount } })` passes on the fresh state, extending dueAt and incrementing renewedCount a SECOND time. (checkout is caught by loans_one_active_per_copy; most returns by the on_loan status CAS — renew is the unprotected one.)
impact: A queued circulation action that already succeeded can be applied twice after a >24h offline gap. Renew double-extends the due date and over-counts renewals past maxRenewals; an over-billed/under-tracked loan results. Precondition-heavy (lost response + >24h offline) but fully silent — the librarian sees a 'synced' toast.
fix: Either (a) cap offline-queue entry age (drop entries older than RESULT_TTL_SEC on flush and warn the librarian to re-verify), keeping it strictly below the server TTL; or (b) make the server idempotency RESULT_TTL_SEC effectively unbounded for these routes / persist the dedup record durably (DB) rather than only in Redis; and add a renewedCount/dueAt-aware guard so a stale renew replay is a no-op.

title: Idempotency PENDING marker (60s TTL) can expire while the handler is still running, letting a concurrent duplicate re-run a non-idempotent circulation op (double fine/return)
evidence: `PENDING_TTL_SEC = 60`. On a won claim the handler runs and only on the success `tap` is the key overwritten with the 24h result (lines 80-86). If the handler takes longer than 60s — a slow tenant DB, a contended advisory lock in the loans return/promotion transaction, or a slow checkout — the `__pending__` key EXPIRES mid-flight. A duplicate request (the offline circulation queue replaying, or an impatient double-submit) then SETNX-succeeds because the key is gone (line 69 returns 'OK'), wins its OWN claim, and re-runs the handler. The interceptor's stated purpose (header doc lines 31-32) is to stop "a returned-twice double fine".
impact: Under DB slowness or lock contention, the exact double-action the interceptor was built to prevent (return-twice double fine, double checkout) can still occur on the offline-replay / double-submit path. Low frequency (needs a >60s handler) but it defeats a data-integrity guard on money-affecting routes.
fix: Either (a) raise/refresh the pending TTL while the handler runs (periodic PEXPIRE / longer PENDING_TTL_SEC sized to the route's worst-case latency), or (b) make the protection robust to a lost lock by ensuring the underlying loan/fine writes are themselves keyed for idempotency. At minimum set PENDING_TTL_SEC comfortably above the slowest expected circulation transaction.

title: Controller cancel/expire promotion path lacks the per-book advisory lock + head-promotion CAS, allowing a stranded 'reserved' copy
evidence: resolveReservation() opens client.$transaction WITHOUT pg_advisory_xact_lock (compare loans.service.ts:418 and reservation-expiry.job.ts:112 which both lock `book:<id>`). promoteNextHoldInTx selects head via plain findFirst and promotes with `tx.reservation.update({ where: { id: head.id }, data: { status:'ready', fulfilledByCopyId } })` — an id-only update, NO `status:'queued'` CAS. The copy flip IS CAS-guarded (updateMany where status='available') but on DIFFERENT copies for concurrent callers.
impact: On a multi-copy book, two concurrent promotions that DON'T mutually exclude (controller force-expire/cancel has no lock; cron expiry job holds book:<id>; a second controller cancel has no lock) each free a different copy (C1, C2) and both flip it available->reserved. Both id-only updates to the same head reservation R succeed (last-writer-wins), so R points at only one copy; the other copy is left status='reserved' with no reservation referencing it -> stranded forever (no expiry job frees an orphaned reserved copy), permanently reducing availability until manual DB repair.
repro: Book with >=2 copies and a queue. Concurrently: (a) librarian force-expires a ready hold via the admin/controller endpoint, and (b) the reservation-expiry cron promotes, OR two controller cancels of two ready holds. Different lock domains -> no mutual exclusion -> double promotion.
fix: In resolveReservation's transaction, take the same advisory lock as the other paths BEFORE promoting: `await tx.$executeRaw\`SELECT pg_advisory_xact_lock(hashtextextended(${`book:${existing.bookId}`}, 0))\`;` Additionally harden promoteNextHoldInTx to a CAS head-promotion: `const promoted = await tx.reservation.updateMany({ where: { id: head.id, status: 'queued' }, data: {...} }); if (promoted.count === 0) return null;` so even an unlocked caller can't double-promote one head. NOTE: the return path (loans:418) and cron job (expiry:112) lock `book:<id>` while hold PLACEMENT (reservations:189) and import (import-engine:651) lock `reservation:<id>` — confirm whether placement-vs-promotion ever need to mutually exclude; placement only allocates when liveCount===0 so today they operate in disjoint queue states, but the inconsistent key is a latent footgun worth unifying.

title: Unsigned desktop builds apply unsigned auto-updates (verifyUpdateCodeSignature=false)
evidence: When Azure signing secrets are absent the release workflow passes --config.win.verifyUpdateCodeSignature=false so electron-updater applies unsigned updates; macOS builds are currently ad-hoc-signed/un-notarized (recent commits). Update integrity then rests solely on TLS + GitHub Releases + the release token.
impact: For unsigned builds, anyone able to publish to the GitHub Releases feed (compromised DESKTOP_RELEASE_TOKEN or repo) can push a malicious auto-update to the entire fleet; there is no code-signature gate. Production fleets should ship signed+notarized builds before GA.
fix: Before GA, provision real code-signing (Apple Developer ID + notarization; Windows Azure Trusted Signing) so verifyUpdateCodeSignature stays ON. Until then, document that unsigned auto-update trusts the release channel and tightly restrict who can publish releases + rotate the release token.

title: Admin-side session epoch (sessionsValidAfter) is read by the guard but never written anywhere
evidence: AdminAuthGuard reads admin.sessionsValidAfter and rejects tokens with `session.iat < validAfterMs/1000`. But a repo-wide grep for writes shows the column is never set: the only adminUser writes are recordFailure/recordSuccess (admin-auth.service.ts:85,91,104) and MFA enrolment (mfa.controller.ts:96) — none touch sessionsValidAfter. There is also no in-app admin password-change or admin-disable endpoint (admins are seed-managed), so the AUTH-01 'forced reset terminates existing admin sessions' guarantee documented in the guard comment (lines 21-23) cannot actually fire.
impact: Defense-in-depth that is effectively dead code today. Not exploitable now (a disabled admin is still caught by the status/disabledAt checks at lines 46-48, which run every request), but if an admin password-reset/rotation feature is added later without remembering to bump this column + nothing forces existing admin cookies (1h TTL) to die, the 'kill existing sessions on reset' expectation silently won't hold.
fix: Either remove the unused branch to avoid a false sense of coverage, or — preferably before shipping any admin self-service password/credential change — wire that path to set adminUser.sessionsValidAfter = now() so the existing read becomes meaningful. Add a regression test asserting a post-reset admin cookie is rejected.

title: Impersonation JWT verify trusts the decoded payload shape without per-claim type checks
evidence: verify() does `jwt.verify(...) as ImpersonationPayload | undefined` and only checks `payload.imp === true`, then returns the cast object. The tenant and admin verifiers (jwt-session.service.ts:84-92, admin-session.service.ts:44-53) explicitly validate the type of every claim (sub/tid/role/iat/exp) per the AUTH-10 hardening — this one does not.
impact: Not exploitable in practice: the token is HMAC-signed with a dedicated impersonationSecret, and ImpersonationMiddleware (impersonation.middleware.ts:49-63) re-loads the SupportSession row by sessionId and cross-checks tenantId/adminId against the payload, so a malformed/forged payload is rejected downstream. It is, however, an inconsistency with the codebase's own AUTH-10 contract and would matter if any consumer ever trusts the payload before the DB cross-check.
fix: Mirror the other two verifiers: validate typeof sub/adminId/tenantId/sessionId === 'string', imp === true, and iat/exp are numbers; return null otherwise instead of casting.

title: Staff first-login (complete-setup) allows a 4-character password
evidence: CompleteSetupDto.newPassword is `@Length(4, 200)`, vs the 12-char minimum enforced on signup (signup.dto.ts:32) and password reset (password-reset.dto.ts:24). login.service.ts completeSetup() hashes whatever is supplied with no extra strength check.
impact: A staff member completing first-login setup can set a 4-char password, which is brute-forceable offline if the control-DB password hashes ever leak and is well below the floor applied everywhere else. Mitigated by per-account login lockout and that staff use usernames within one tenant, so it is low severity, but it's an inconsistent and weak floor for an interactive login credential.
fix: Raise the complete-setup newPassword minimum to match the rest of the product (e.g. @MinLength(12)), or at least to a defensible interactive-login floor (>=8). If short staff PINs are intentional, document the threat model; otherwise align the DTO.

title: Tenant session relies on SameSite=Lax alone — no CSRF token, no defense in depth
evidence: The tenant session cookie is set with `sameSite: 'lax'` (lines 32, 43) and there is no CSRF token anywhere in apps/web or apps/api (grep for csrf/xsrf returns nothing). All state-changing browser calls are JSON POST/PATCH/DELETE via the same-origin /lbr-api proxy with credentials:'include' (apps/web/lib/api.ts:88-98). I confirmed there is NO CORS configured on the API (no enableCors in apps/api/src/main.ts) and found no state-changing @Get endpoints, so a cross-site request cannot both send the Lax cookie and reach a mutating handler today. Admin and impersonation cookies correctly use SameSite=Strict (admin-cookie.service.ts:26, impersonation-cookie.service.ts:24), so only the tenant plane is on the weaker Lax setting.
impact: Not exploitable as written: SameSite=Lax suppresses the cookie on cross-site POST, and with no CORS a cross-origin credentialed XHR is blocked, so there is no working CSRF path. The risk is purely defense-in-depth — a future regression that adds a permissive CORS policy, a top-level GET that mutates state, or a same-site subdomain takeover would have no second line of defense for tenant write operations.
fix: Add a standard double-submit or header-based CSRF defense for the tenant plane (e.g. require a non-cookie custom header such as X-Requested-With / X-CSRF on all mutating routes — trivial to enforce since all browser writes already go through lib/api.ts and could add the header centrally), and/or tighten the tenant session to SameSite=Strict like the admin/impersonation cookies if the UX (no cross-site top-level entry needed) allows it.

title: Over-broad macOS hardened-runtime entitlements (audio-input granted though unused; library validation + unsigned-exec memory disabled)
evidence: Entitlements include `com.apple.security.cs.disable-library-validation`, `com.apple.security.cs.allow-unsigned-executable-memory`, and `com.apple.security.device.audio-input` (true). The audio entitlement contradicts the code's own intent — extendInfo in electron-builder.yml:63 states 'Libriant only needs the camera; microphone access is not used.' and the permission allowlist (main.ts:283) does not include microphone-specific media beyond what camera needs. disable-library-validation lets unsigned/third-party dylibs load into the signed app.
impact: Weakens the hardened-runtime guarantees more than necessary: an attacker who achieves local code-injection has an easier time loading unsigned libraries, and the unused mic entitlement grants the app microphone access (privacy surface) for no functional reason. JIT/allow-jit and allow-unsigned-executable-memory are genuinely required by V8; library-validation and audio-input are the questionable ones.
fix: Remove com.apple.security.device.audio-input (the scanner uses the camera only). Re-evaluate com.apple.security.cs.disable-library-validation — Electron typically does not require it; drop it unless a notarization failure proves otherwise. Keep allow-jit/allow-unsigned-executable-memory (V8 needs them).

title: Deploy health gate hits Caddy's static always-200 /healthz, not app health — a stack that crashes after `up` is reported healthy and auto-rollback never fires
evidence: deploy.yml:321 `code="$(curl -sS -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}' --max-time 5 http://localhost/healthz ...)"` is the only post-deploy gate that triggers the `if: failure()` rollback step (deploy.yml:333-336). In the Caddyfile the plaintext :80 site answers that path with a static literal: `http:// { @probe path /healthz /readyz; handle @probe { respond "ok" 200 } ... }` (Caddyfile:115-119) — it never proxies to api or web. So the gate returns 200 whenever the Caddy container is up, independent of whether api/web/worker actually stayed healthy. The step's own comment (deploy.yml:305-313) claims it verifies 'the new code came up'. The real gate is `docker compose ... up -d` failing on `depends_on: condition: service_healthy` (deploy.yml:288), but that only checks health at the instant of `up`; a container that passes start_period then crash-loops (runtime error under load, flapping /readyz) is not caught here.
impact: The documented DR guarantee 'production never stays on a broken build — the host is AUTOMATICALLY rolled back' (deploy.yml:148-152) does not hold for a deploy whose app comes up momentarily then fails. Operators get a green deploy and a down/degraded site, with no auto-rollback and no alert from this gate.
fix: Probe real app health through the proxy instead of Caddy's literal: poll the api's readiness, e.g. `docker compose exec -T api wget -qO- http://localhost:3001/readyz` (the api container's own healthcheck target, compose:192) and the web's `/api/healthz`, on the host over the existing SSH session. Keep the static :80 /healthz only for the load-balancer liveness probe, not as the deploy success criterion.

adversarial.reason: The claim's central premise is refuted by the compose file. It asserts the Caddy static /healthz (Caddyfile:115-119, deploy.yml:321) is "the only post-deploy gate" and that `docker compose up -d` "only checks health at the instant of up." Both are false. In infra/compose/docker-compose.prod.yml the deploy actually gates on real application healthchecks via `depends_on: condition: service_healthy`: api (line 105-106 / 191-196) is probed at http://localhost:3001/readyz (15s interval, 8 retries, 30s start_period), web (line 103-104 / 224-229) at http://localhost:3000/api/healthz, and caddy (line 102-106) depends on BOTH being healthy. `up -d --force-recreate` (deploy.yml:288) blocks until those conditions are satisfied — it waits for the app readiness probes, it does not merely sample at the instant of up. So a deploy where api/web fail to come up exits non-zero, triggering the `if: failure()` rollback (deploy.yml:333-336). The DR guarantee (deploy.yml:149-152) therefore DOES hold for a build that fails to start. The author misread the gate: the Caddy /healthz poll (Wait for health step) is a secondary check whose stated purpose (deploy.yml:318-320) is to confirm the Caddy config RELOAD at line 299 took effect (new config = 200, stale config = 301-to-HTTPS), not to be the app-health gate. The only residual is the generic "container passes start_period then crash-loops under later production load" gap — but that is a universal property of every service_healthy-gated deploy, is not specific to the Caddy literal probe, and is explicitly scoped to uptime monitoring rather than the deploy gate by the code's own comment (deploy.yml:313). Runtime crashes are also mitigated by container healthchecks + restart:unless-stopped. Net: the impactful failure mode the claim describes (broken build reported healthy, no rollback) does not occur for a deploy that fails to come up; the narrow residual is a known, documented monitoring boundary, not a high-severity ops/DR defect.

title: hono / @hono/node-server (9 advisories) — dev-only via @prisma/dev, AWS-Lambda/Windows-specific, not in runtime path
evidence: `pnpm why hono -r` and `pnpm why @hono/node-server -r` show the ONLY paths are @prisma/client@7.8.0 > prisma@7.8.0 > @prisma/dev@0.24.3 > (@hono/node-server@1.19.11 / hono@4.12.23). @prisma/dev is Prisma's local development server tool; it is not imported or executed by the running API (the API uses @prisma/client + @prisma/adapter-pg against Postgres). The 8 hono advisories (GHSA-88fw-hqm2-52qc CORS wildcard, -wwfh-h76j-fc44 Windows %5C traversal in serve-static, plus 6 AWS-Lambda/Lambda@Edge adapter bugs) and @hono/node-server GHSA-92pp-h63x-v22m all require either the hono HTTP server to be the app's edge server or an AWS Lambda deployment — neither is true for Libriant (NestJS/Express on Node).
impact: No production exposure: the vulnerable hono server code never runs in Libriant's request path. Will clear automatically when Prisma ships @prisma/dev with hono >=4.12.25.
fix: No action strictly required. To silence the audit, either wait for a prisma patch release or add pnpm.overrides "hono": ">=4.12.25" and "@hono/node-server": ">=1.19.13" (low risk since the code is unused, but verify prisma generate/dev still works locally).

title: nodemailer 8.0.9 (prod dep) — vulnerable `raw` option never used; EMAIL_DRIVER=console in prod
evidence: GHSA-p6gq-j5cr-w38f targets nodemailer's message-level `raw` option bypassing disableFileAccess/disableUrlAccess (arbitrary file read / SSRF). The only call site, smtp-driver.ts:50-60, builds the message from `{ from, to, replyTo, subject, text: input.bodyMarkdown, html: markdownToBasicHtml(...) }` — it never sets `raw`, never sets attachments with file paths/URLs, and bodies are system-generated markdown templates, not attacker-controlled MIME. Per project memory the prod setting is EMAIL_DRIVER=console (no SMTP transport instantiated). Note env.ts:357 defaults emailDriver to 'smtp' when NODE_ENV!=development, so the driver could be active if the env var were unset, but the vulnerable code path still would not be reachable.
impact: No reachable exploit path. The file-read/SSRF requires the `raw` option which Libriant does not expose.
fix: Bump apps/api dependency to nodemailer ^9.0.1 (patched) at next convenient maintenance; not blocking for go-live. Keep EMAIL_DRIVER=console until the Resend key is available (per memory).

title: /metrics relies solely on Caddy + network topology (no in-app guard) — leaks fleet-wide tenant counts if either layer regresses
evidence: HealthController is `@Controller()` with no @UseGuards; @Get('metrics') (l.61) returns libriant_tenants_total{status}, libriant_storage_used_bytes, pg connection/cache gauges, redis memory — i.e. whole-fleet operational intelligence. The ONLY protection is Caddy `respond @internal 404` for /metrics on the public and admin /lbr-api/* routes (Caddyfile:149,196) plus the api container publishing no host ports. There is no second layer at the app: any process on the shared `app` docker network (e.g. the web container, or a future side-car) can GET http://api:3001/metrics directly and read fleet tenant counts. A single Caddyfile edit/regression silently re-exposes it.
impact: Defense-in-depth gap. Aggregate-only (no per-tenant PII in labels), so impact is limited to leaking total tenant/capacity counts, but it's a single-layer control on data that should be operator-only.
fix: Add a lightweight in-app guard on /metrics (shared-secret bearer token the Prometheus scrape config carries, or bind metrics to a separate internal-only listener). Keeps the Caddy 404 as belt, adds braces.

title: redactSecrets() leaks part of a DB password that contains an '@' character
evidence: redactSecrets = s.replace(/(postgres(?:ql)?:\/\/[^:@/\s]+:)[^@/\s]+@/gi, '$1***@'). The password class [^@/\s]+ stops at the first '@'. Tested: input `pg_dump postgresql://tenant_role:S3cr3tP@ss@db:5432/...` → output `postgresql://tenant_role:***@ss@db:5432/...`, leaking the `ss` tail of the password into the tenant-visible exportJob.error field. Generated DB-role secrets are normally @-free (hex/base64url), so this only bites if a password (e.g. an operator-set superuser password in a connection URL) contains '@'.
impact: Partial credential disclosure into the tenant-readable job.error field, but only for passwords containing '@' (uncommon for generated secrets; possible for operator-chosen superuser creds). Low real-world likelihood.
fix: Anchor to the last '@' before host or strip the whole userinfo: e.g. replace(/(postgres(?:ql)?:\/\/)[^@\s]*@/gi, '$1***@') so the entire user:pass segment is masked regardless of '@' in the password.

title: Admin-panel host isolation is enforced only in the Next.js web layer; the admin API has no host/Host-header check and relies solely on the __Host- cookie
file: apps/web/app/[locale]/admin/layout.tsx:28-34 (API side: apps/api/src/admin/admin-auth.guard.ts:29-64, no host check anywhere in /admin/* controllers)
evidence: Commit cd7c9cb added the only host gate, in the web layout: `const adminHost=(process.env.ADMIN_HOST??'')...; if(reqHost && reqHost!==adminHost) notFound();`. The API admin controllers (`@Controller('admin/...')`) are matched on ANY host; AdminAuthGuard authenticates purely from the signed `__Host-libriant_admin` cookie (admin-auth.guard.ts:31-45) with no Host comparison. The commit message asserts 'the admin API was unreachable cross-host' but that property comes only from the cookie's __Host- prefix (env.ts:272-275, set with path:'/' and no Domain in admin-cookie.service.ts:22-30), not from any API-side host enforcement.
impact: The defense currently holds because a __Host- cookie set on admin.<apex> is never sent to the public apex, so /admin/* on the public host gets 401. But the protection is implicit and single-layered: if ADMIN_COOKIE_NAME is ever overridden to drop the __Host- prefix, or a future change loosens the cookie scope/Domain, the admin API becomes reachable on the public host with no second barrier. The web 404 is cosmetic and does not protect the API.
fix: Add a defense-in-depth host check on the API admin surface (a middleware/guard that 404s /admin/* when the request Host !== ADMIN_HOST, mirroring the web layout and the TenantMiddleware adminHost handling at tenant.middleware.ts:121), and add a startup assertion that the admin cookie name retains the __Host- prefix in production. Do not trust X-Forwarded-Host for this — use the validated Host that Caddy preserves.

title: Misleading comment claims a cross-tenant replay check the signed-download endpoint does not (and need not) perform
evidence: JSDoc on verify(): "Caller must STILL check that the request's resolved tenant matches `payload.tid` — defence against a leaked token being used against a different tenant via a forged Host header." But the actual consumer in storage-demo.controller.ts:187-204 (`@Get('_files/signed')`) runs no tenant middleware (the route is not under /t/ and carries no slug), so there is no `req.tenant` to compare. It instead resolves the tenant directly FROM the signed `payload.tid` (resolveTenantById, line 197) and reads `storage.get(tenant, payload.ref)`. That is actually correct and replay-safe (ref+tid are signed together, secret is HMAC-distinct), but the comment describes a check that doesn't exist, inviting a future maintainer to either add a redundant/incorrect check or to wrongly assume one is already enforcing isolation.
impact: Documentation/maintainability risk only. No isolation impact today: a token from tenant A cannot be used to read tenant B because the served tenant is derived from the signed tid, not from any attacker-controllable Host/path.
fix: Rewrite the comment to state that isolation is enforced by deriving the tenant from the signed `tid` (not from request context), since `/_files/signed` runs outside tenant middleware. Remove the 'caller must check resolved tenant' sentence so nobody adds a meaningless or breaking comparison.

title: Announcement dismiss/ack do not verify the announcement targets the caller's tenant (write-safe, but allows no-op cross-tenant probes)
evidence: dismiss() and acknowledge() look up the announcement by id only (`controlDb.announcement.findUnique({ where: { id: input.announcementId } })`) and never call anns.tenantMatches() to confirm the announcement's audience includes this tenant. They DO scope the write by tenant: `controlDb.announcementDelivery.updateMany({ where: { announcementId, tenantId: input.tenantId, userId } })`. Because the controller (tenant-announcements.controller.ts:48-74) always supplies `tenantId: tenant.id` from the resolved TenantContext behind TenantGuard, a cross-tenant write is impossible — updateMany simply matches 0 rows for a foreign tenant/announcement and returns success.
impact: No cross-tenant data write or read. A librarian can POST dismiss/ack for an arbitrary announcement id (incl. one not targeted at their tenant) and get a 200 with zero effect — a minor existence-probe / API-noise issue, not a breach. The 404 'cannot be dismissed' branch already prevents acting on non-dismissible announcements.
fix: For consistency and to return a clean 404 on foreign announcements, gate dismiss/ack on anns.tenantMatches(audienceFromJson(ann.audienceFilter), { id, tags, status }) before the updateMany (the active-set fetcher already does this). Strictly defense-in-depth; not required to close an isolation hole.

title: Admin can enable plan/quota billing at runtime while STRIPE_DRIVER=fake — checkout/portal silently run the in-memory stand-in in production
evidence: billingEnabled() returns the platform_settings DB row when present, else the env default (platform-settings.service.ts:39). The admin 'Subscriptions' toggle writes that row (setBillingEnabled, lines 45-55) with no check on the resolved Stripe driver. Prod compose defaults are independent: `BILLING_ENABLED: ${BILLING_ENABLED:-false}` and `STRIPE_DRIVER: ${STRIPE_DRIVER:-fake}` (compose:61-62). billing.service.ts reports them separately (`driver: this.stripe.isReal ? 'real' : 'fake'`, billing.service.ts:155; `billingEnabled: await this.settings.billingEnabled()`, :156) but never asserts real-driver when enforcement is on.
impact: If an operator flips Subscriptions ON in the admin UI but has not switched STRIPE_DRIVER to real (the default is fake), enforcement gates engage while checkout/customer-portal calls hit the FakeStripeDriver, which returns canned IDs and records no real charge. No security/data breach (webhooks are still HMAC-verified when real), but tenants could be gated/upgraded against a billing backend that never actually charges — a monetization-correctness foot-gun. Low because billing is OFF by default at launch per the roadmap.
fix: When PlatformSettingsService.setBillingEnabled(true) is called, refuse (or loudly warn in the admin UI) unless the resolved Stripe driver isReal; surface a mismatch banner on the Subscriptions admin page.

title: Renew checks for a blocking hold outside any transaction/lock — a hold placed in the check→update window lets the loan renew past it
evidence: renew is the only state-changing loan op with NO `client.$transaction` and no advisory lock. It reads `const queuedHold = await client.reservation.findFirst({ where: { bookId: loan.copy.bookId, status: { in: ['queued','ready'] } } })` (lines 612-615) and refuses if found, then later issues a separate `client.loan.updateMany(... renewedCount CAS ...)` (lines 632-635). Between the read and the write a concurrent placeHold (which locks only `reservation:${bookId}`, a different namespace) can insert a queued hold; renew has already passed its 'no hold waiting' check and proceeds to extend dueAt. The renewedCount CAS protects against double-renew but does nothing about a hold that appeared after the hold-check.
impact: A member can renew and keep a book even though someone just got in line for it, contrary to the documented policy ('you can't renew while there's an active hold'). Self-correcting over time (the hold is promoted on the next return/expiry) so no corruption — purely a fairness/policy violation in a narrow race window.
fix: Wrap the hold-check and the renew CAS in a single transaction that first takes the per-book advisory lock (same `book:${bookId}` key as the promotion paths), so a concurrent placeHold serializes against the renew decision.

title: User-supplied multiSeparators is interpolated into a character class without escaping '-', causing whole-batch crash or silent data mangling
evidence: splitMulti builds `new RegExp('[' + separators.replace(/[.*+?^${}()[\]\\]/g,'\\$&') + ']')`. The escape set omits '-'. Verified at runtime: multiSeparators='z-a' throws `Invalid regular expression: /[z-a]/: Range out of order in character class`, and multiSeparators='a-z' silently builds `[a-z]` so splitMulti('Hello World','a-z') returns ['H','W'] — splitting on every letter instead of the literal chars a, -, z. multiSeparators flows in unvalidated except `typeof === 'string'` (import.service.ts:319 cleanOptions). The throw is uncaught in mapRow→applyTransform (row-mapper.ts:136) and propagates to executeImport (runner.ts:55, no per-row try/catch) up to the worker catch (import-worker.ts:198), failing the ENTIRE batch rather than one row.
impact: Self-inflicted (owner/admin sets the mapping option), so low severity. The 'Range out of order' variant fails an otherwise-clean batch with an opaque error; the unescaped-'-' variant silently corrupts imported multi-valued data (authors etc.) by splitting on character ranges with no per-row issue raised.
fix: Add '-' to the escaped character set (`/[-.*+?^${}()[\]\\]/g`), or build the alternation from individually-escaped single characters rather than a character class. Wrap the RegExp construction in try/catch and surface a precise per-field issue instead of letting it abort the run.

title: Email worker re-sends on a crash between provider send and the 'delivered' DB write (at-least-once with no provider-side dedup)
evidence: processOne only short-circuits when `row.status === 'delivered' || 'dead'` (line 111). The flow flips the row to 'sending' (line 115), calls driver.send (line 121), THEN writes 'delivered' (line 128). If the worker crashes (or is force-exited by the 25s shutdown deadline) after driver.send succeeds but before line 128, BullMQ's stalled-job recovery re-delivers the job; the row is still 'sending', so processOne proceeds and re-sends. No Idempotency-Key / dedup is sent to Resend or SMTP.
impact: A patron/library can receive a duplicate of any outbox email (overdue nag, hold-ready, password reset) after a worker crash or a forced shutdown that interrupts an in-flight send. At-least-once email is generally tolerable, so impact is limited to occasional duplicate mail.
fix: Send a stable idempotency token to the provider (Resend supports an Idempotency-Key header; SMTP can reuse a stable Message-ID derived from the outbox id) so the provider dedups a re-sent row, or accept and document the at-least-once semantics.

title: Scheduled-jobs runner shares one Redis connection between the BullMQ Queue (producer) and the blocking Worker
evidence: A single `const connection = new Redis(...)` is passed to both `new Queue(QUEUE_NAME, { connection, ... })` (line 42) and `new Worker(QUEUE_NAME, ..., { connection, ... })` (line 111). BullMQ Workers issue blocking commands on their connection; sharing that socket with a Queue producer is a documented BullMQ anti-pattern. The other workers (email/import/export/maintenance) correctly give the Worker its own socket and keep the producer Queue elsewhere.
impact: Mostly benign here because the scheduled Queue is only used at boot (reconcile + register repeatables) and is otherwise idle, so production impact is minimal. Could cause command stalls if the Queue were used at runtime; flagged for correctness/consistency.
fix: Give the scheduled Worker its own ioredis connection separate from the Queue's (duplicate the connection or pass a connection factory), matching the pattern in email-worker.ts / EmailService.

title: Desktop shell accepts any http:// (not just https) server URL from env/config
evidence: isValidHttpUrl returns true for protocol 'http:' OR 'https:'. LIBRIANT_APP_URL env and persisted config.serverUrl are accepted as-is and become appOrigin. setServerUrl (main.ts:293) persists any valid http(s) URL.
impact: An attacker who can write the per-user config file (userData/libriant-desktop.json) or set LIBRIANT_APP_URL can repoint the shell at an attacker-controlled http origin, which then becomes the 'trusted' appOrigin for the IPC bridge (setServerUrl, open-external, same-origin /print/). Not RCE (sandbox + contextIsolation + nodeIntegration off; install-update requires an update already downloaded from the SIGNED GitHub feed), but enables persistent redirection/phishing and MITM on plain http.
repro: Set config.serverUrl to http://evil.example and relaunch; the shell loads it and treats it as trusted.
fix: For packaged builds, require https:// (allow http only when !app.isPackaged for localhost dev), or constrain to an allowlist/the DEFAULT_APP_URL host. Optionally sign/validate the config file. Low because writing userData or env already implies local access.

title: CSP allows 'unsafe-inline' for script-src, weakening XSS containment
evidence: The CSP sets `script-src 'self' 'unsafe-inline'` (and style-src 'unsafe-inline'), acknowledged in the comment as needed because 'the App Router emits [bootstrap/hydration inline scripts] without a nonce'. object-src 'none', base-uri 'self', frame-ancestors 'none', and connect-src 'self' are correctly locked down.
impact: If an HTML-injection sink ever regresses (the code does use dangerouslySetInnerHTML for the token <style>, print CSS, and help-article HTML), 'unsafe-inline' on script-src means an injected inline <script> would execute — the CSP would not contain it. No such sink is currently reachable with user input (verified: all three dangerouslySetInnerHTML sources are server-controlled), so this is hardening, not an active vulnerability.
fix: Move to a nonce-based CSP via request-scoped middleware so 'unsafe-inline' can be dropped from script-src (Next.js App Router supports nonce propagation through middleware). At minimum keep the help-article ingest pipeline (the one HTML sink that renders rendered markdown) sanitized/whitelisted so it can never emit <script> regardless of CSP.

title: Server URL may be plain HTTP — session cookie and all traffic sent in cleartext, no HTTPS enforcement
evidence: isValidHttpUrl accepts http: as well as https: — config.ts:25 `return u.protocol === 'http:' || u.protocol === 'https:';`. This validator gates every URL source: LIBRIANT_APP_URL env, the persisted serverUrl, and the renderer/fallback-driven setServerUrl (main.ts:293 `if (!isValidHttpUrl(url)) return ...; config.serverUrl = url; ... loadAppUrl(url);`). openExternal likewise allows http: (main.ts:97). Nothing upgrades or requires https for the loaded app origin; the default is https (config.ts:11) but any override can be cleartext. The shell carries the librarian's authenticated session cookie (silentPrint relies on it riding along: main.ts:115-119).
impact: An operator pointing the shell at an http:// instance (on-prem, LAN, a typo, or a setServerUrl call) transmits the session cookie and all library data over cleartext. A network attacker on the LAN can steal the session, read/modify circulation data, and inject a page into the (sandboxed, but cookie-bearing) renderer. No warning is surfaced. This is a transport-downgrade exposure that a browser would at least flag; the shell silently accepts it.
fix: For production targets, require https for the loaded app origin (allow http only for localhost/dev or behind an explicit opt-in flag). At minimum, refuse http URLs in setServerUrl when app.isPackaged, and surface a clear insecure-connection warning in the fallback/connection UI.

adversarial.reason:
Code reading confirms the literal facts (config.ts:25 isValidHttpUrl accepts http: and https:; main.ts:293-299 setServerUrl has no app.isPackaged/localhost guard; main.ts:97 openExternal allows http:), but the "high" framing is overstated and not attacker-exploitable on the running product.

Why it is not a real high finding:
1. Not attacker-reachable. setServerUrl is gated by isTrustedSender (main.ts:87-92, 415-417): only the app-origin top frame or the bundled file:// fallback can invoke it. The renderer is sandboxed (sandbox:true, contextIsolation:true, nodeIntegration:false), navigation is pinned to appOrigin (will-navigate, will-attach-webview prevented), and preload.ts exposes only a tiny audited surface. A network/LAN MITM has no primitive to flip a victim from https to http. So there is no "downgrade" an attacker can drive — only operator configuration.
2. The precondition is a deliberate operator/IT choice, not an exploit. Pointing the shell at a chosen server (env LIBRIANT_APP_URL, config JSON, or the fallback connection UI) is the intended self-hosting/on-prem override. http://localhost:3000 is the documented dev default (config.ts:12); the packaged default is https://libriant.com (config.ts:11). Running an on-prem LAN instance over http is a supported operator decision, equivalent to a browser visiting an http site.
3. The actual cleartext-cookie control is server-side, not in the desktop shell. Cookies are set with secure: env.sessionCookieSecure (apps/api/src/auth/cookie.service.ts:13-42 and the admin/impersonation cookie services). For the hosted product the Secure flag is on, so the session cookie will not traverse http at all regardless of what URL the shell loads. Cleartext session exposure requires an operator to BOTH serve over http AND set sessionCookieSecure=false — a self-inflicted self-hosted misconfiguration, not a product vulnerability.
4. The "a browser would flag it" argument is inaccurate: browsers load http origins and transmit non-Secure cookies over them without blocking.

This is a legitimate defense-in-depth hardening idea (refuse/ warn on http for app.isPackaged builds, allow http only for localhost or an explicit opt-in), but it is a low/info hardening nit, not a serious issue with a reachable precondition or DR/ops impact. Marking real=false at the claimed severity; adjusted to info.

title: Silent printing requires no user consent once the renderer is trusted
evidence: The print bridge drives wc.print({ silent: true, printBackground: true }) (main.ts:170) on a same-origin /print/ route with no per-action user confirmation. It is well-constrained (top-frame + origin gated, same-origin + /print/ path only, no caller fragment, preload-less hidden window, 20s teardown timeout) so it cannot print arbitrary pages or write arbitrary files.
impact: A compromised trusted renderer could spam the default printer with same-origin /print/ routes (paper/toner waste / nuisance), but cannot read files, print arbitrary content, or escape the sandbox. Acceptable for a kiosk circulation desk; noting as residual surface, not a defect.
fix: No change required. If desired, rate-limit silentPrint calls per minute to blunt nuisance abuse.

title: qs — vulnerable 6.14.2 is dev-only (supertest); production qs is already patched 6.15.2
evidence: `pnpm why qs -r`: production path is @nestjs/platform-express > express@5.2.1 > body-parser/qs@6.15.2, which is ABOVE the advisory range (GHSA-q8mj-m7cp-5q26 affects >=6.11.1 <=6.15.1). The only vulnerable copy is qs@6.14.2 under devDependencies supertest > superagent (test client). The DoS would only fire in test code calling qs.stringify with comma-format arrays + encodeValuesOnly.
impact: No production exposure; the runtime querystring parser is patched.
fix: No action needed for prod. The dev copy clears when supertest/superagent updates; optionally pnpm.overrides "qs": ">=6.15.2".

title: form-data <4.0.6 — dev/build-tool only (supertest + electron-builder), not a runtime dependency
evidence: `pnpm why form-data -r` shows all three paths are non-runtime: apps/api devDependencies @types/supertest and supertest>superagent>form-data@4.0.5, and apps/desktop devDependencies electron-builder>app-builder-lib>electron-publish>form-data@4.0.5. No production code (NestJS API, Next web, Electron main) depends on form-data. The CRLF-injection (GHSA-hmw2-7cc7-3qxx) needs an HTTP client building multipart bodies with attacker-controlled field names — only test/release tooling does that here.
impact: No runtime exposure. Worst case is during local test runs or desktop release packaging, both trusted-input contexts.
fix: No action needed for production. Will resolve as supertest/electron-builder update; optionally pnpm.overrides "form-data": ">=4.0.6".

title: postcss 8.4.31 (bundled in next) — build-time only, not required under next/dist/server
evidence: `pnpm why postcss -r`: prod path is apps/web > next@16.2.6 > postcss@8.4.31; other path (vite/vitest) is dev. GHSA-qx2v-qp2m-jg93 is XSS via unescaped </style> in postcss's CSS-stringify output, which requires processing untrusted CSS at runtime. Grep of node_modules/.pnpm/next@16.2.6/node_modules/next/dist/server/ for require('postcss')/from 'postcss' returns nothing — postcss is used only at `next build` to compile the app's own (trusted) CSS, not in the running server.
impact: No production exposure: no untrusted CSS is ever passed through postcss at runtime.
fix: No action needed; clears when Next bumps its bundled postcss. (postcss is internal to next, not separately installable, so an override on the top-level postcss only affects the dev/vite copy.)

title: uuid 8.3.2 (via exceljs) — vulnerable buf-bounds path unreachable; only uuid.v4() is called
evidence: `pnpm why uuid -r`: apps/api > exceljs@4.4.0 > uuid@8.3.2. GHSA-w5hq-g745-h8pq is a missing buffer bounds check in v3/v5/v6 only when a `buf` argument is supplied. exceljs's only usage (node_modules/.pnpm/exceljs@4.4.0/.../cf-rule-ext-xform.js:1 `const {v4: uuidv4} = require('uuid')`, calls `uuidv4()` with no args) uses random v4 with no buffer argument, so the vulnerable code path is never exercised.
impact: No exposure; the vulnerable function/argument combination is never called.
fix: No action needed; clears when exceljs updates uuid.

title: vite / launch-editor / esbuild — build/test tooling only, Windows-dev-server-specific
evidence: `pnpm why vite -r` and `pnpm why esbuild -r`: vite@7.3.3 comes only via apps/api devDependency vitest@4.1.7; esbuild@0.28.0/0.27.7 only via tsx and vitest/vite (all dev/build). Advisories GHSA-fx2h-pf6j-xcff (vite server.fs.deny bypass on Windows), GHSA-v6wh-96g9-6wx3 (launch-editor NTLM hash disclosure on Windows), GHSA-g7r4-m6w7-qqqr (esbuild dev-server arbitrary file read on Windows) all require running a dev server, on Windows, exposed to a malicious request — none of which is part of Libriant's production runtime or its Linux CI/build.
impact: No production exposure. Risk is limited to a developer running the dev server on Windows with a hostile local network — not the deployed app.
fix: No action needed for go-live. Bump vitest/tsx to pull vite>=7.3.5 and esbuild>=0.28.1 at routine maintenance to clear the audit noise.

title: pnpm overrides + lockfile + install scripts — verified safe
evidence: Root package.json pnpm.overrides pins react ^19.2.6, react-dom ^19.2.6, ioredis ^5.11.0; pnpm-lock.yaml resolves react@19.2.6, react-dom@19.2.6(react@19.2.6), ioredis@5.11.0 — all current, none flagged in G11. `pnpm install --frozen-lockfile` => "Lockfile is up to date" / "Already up to date" (matches package.json, G1 frozen-lockfile corroborated). No .npmrc and no onlyBuiltDependencies allowlist exist, so pnpm 9 blocks postinstall/build scripts of dependencies by default; no apps/* or packages/* package.json declares preinstall/postinstall/install scripts; production deps are pure-JS (bcryptjs, not native bcrypt — no node-gyp build at install).
impact: No supply-chain install-time code-execution surface introduced by the project config; overrides are current.
fix: No change required. Optionally add an explicit pnpm.onlyBuiltDependencies allowlist to make build-script policy intentional rather than relying on the default.

title: export-worker logs raw err.message (possibly an unredacted connection string) to operator stdout
evidence: `worker.on('failed', (job, err) => console.error(`[export-worker] job ${job?.id} failed: ${err.message}`))`. The export-processors path redacts secrets before persisting to the DB (job.error), but this BullMQ failure handler logs the raw err.message to stderr/container logs. A pg_dump/connection failure message can include `postgresql://user:pass@host`, so a tenant DB credential could land unredacted in operator-visible container logs (not tenant-visible).
impact: Operator-only log exposure of a tenant/superuser DB credential on export failure. Container logs are access-controlled, so impact is limited to log-aggregation surface.
fix: Run the existing redactSecrets() over err.message in the worker failed handlers (export-worker.ts:41 and similar in import/email/maintenance workers) before logging.

title: GET /t/:slug/plan and /plan/usage (effective-plan + raw override internals) are reachable by any tenant role including volunteer, but are 404'd in production by NonProductionOnlyGuard
evidence: PlanDemoController is `@UseGuards(NonProductionOnlyGuard, TenantGuard, PlanGuard)` and the guard returns 404 outside development (`private readonly enabled = loadEnv().nodeEnv !== 'production'; if(this.enabled) return true; throw new NotFoundException()`). The guard is listed FIRST so prod requests 404 before TenantGuard warms a pool. Verified nodeEnv defaults to non-production only when NODE_ENV is unset; in prod NODE_ENV=production so these routes are absent.
impact: None in production (routes 404). Noted only because the plan/usage read has no @Roles even in dev and exposes plan-source internals; confirm NODE_ENV=production is actually set for the API service at deploy time (the project has a documented web-side NODE_ENV gotcha) so this guard's enabled flag computes false.
fix: No action required if NODE_ENV=production is guaranteed for the API container. Optionally fail-closed: have NonProductionOnlyGuard treat an unrecognized/empty NODE_ENV as production rather than dev, so a missing env var hides the demo routes instead of exposing them.

title: Tenant-status reactivation has no cache-invalidation hook, but no reactivation endpoint exists yet (TEN-04 latent)
evidence: The resolver positively caches the full TenantContext including `status` for tenantCacheTtlSec; the middleware (tenant.middleware.ts:76-83) enforces archived→410 / suspended→403 AFTER reading the cache. invalidate() exists and is called by hard-delete (admin-tenants.controller.ts:200-202), tags (admin-tenant-tags.controller.ts:75-78) and relocate (scripts/tenant-relocate.ts:462-464). I found NO admin/billing code path that flips tenants.status to suspended/archived/active (grep for tenant.update/updateMany shows only brandColor/brandLogoRef and tags writes; billing past_due acts on Subscription.status + EffectivePlan, not Tenant.status). So today the cached status is always consistent with the row.
impact: Latent only: if a suspend/archive/reactivate endpoint is added later WITHOUT calling resolver.invalidate(), every API process would serve the stale status for up to the TTL — a suspended tenant could keep being served, or a reactivated one stay locked out. Not exploitable now because the mutation surface doesn't exist.
fix: When implementing tenant suspend/archive/reactivate (and any billing→tenant.status transition), call TenantResolverService.invalidate({ slug, customSubdomain }) in the same operation, mirroring the existing tags/relocate/delete callers. Consider a control-plane test asserting any tenants.status write is paired with an invalidate.

title: OpenLibrary outbound fetch is not SSRF-exploitable
evidence: URL host is hardcoded `https://openlibrary.org/...` and the only injected value is `${isbn}` where isbn = digitsOnly(rawIsbn) (normalize.ts:42-46 strips everything except 0-9Xx) and must pass isValidIsbnShape (len 10 or 13). fetch uses `redirect: 'manual'` (openlibrary.ts:54) so a 3xx to a cloud-metadata/internal address is never chased, a 5s AbortController timeout (line 46), and readCappedJson enforces MAX_RESPONSE_BYTES=1_000_000 (lines 73,84,106).
impact: No attacker-controlled host/path; cannot reach internal addresses or metadata endpoints. Documented as verified-clean, not a vulnerability.
fix: No change needed.

title: Local storage driver and signed-URL ref handling block path traversal
evidence: safeResolve rejects null bytes, any `..` or empty path segment, and verifies `candidate === this.root || candidate.startsWith(this.root + sep)` (local-driver.ts:112-119); requireSafe throws EPERM otherwise. Stored filenames are server-generated (cuidLike + whitelisted extension, lines 55-57,134-153). title: No SQL injection, command injection, or XXE in raw SQL / pg_dump / XML parsing
evidence: All $executeRaw/$queryRaw use Prisma tagged templates with ${} bound params (loans.service.ts:446-452,897-906; storage.service.ts:76-81,196-204; reservations.service.ts:343,515); $queryRawUnsafe sites use $1..$N placeholders + separate args (help.service.ts:79-95, effective-plan.service.ts:143-166) or a literal 'SELECT 1' (maintenance-processors.ts:149). pg_dump runs via execFile (array args, no shell) with credentials in PG* env not argv (export-processors.ts:327-344); readTables interpolates only table names sourced from pg_tables system catalog (export-processors.ts:373). MARCXML uses fast-xml-parser with no DTD/entity expansion (marc-parser.ts:142-149) → no XXE.
impact: No injection vector found across these surfaces. Documented as verified-clean.
fix: No change needed.

title: MFA_MASTER_KEY format (64-hex) is validated at MfaService construction, not at env load
evidence: env.ts only enforces presence in prod (`required('MFA_MASTER_KEY')`) and does not run the 64-hex .validate() that secrets.ts defines for the same key (secrets.ts:170-171). The hex/length check lives in MfaService: `if (!/^[0-9a-fA-F]{64}$/.test(hex)) throw new Error('MFA_MASTER_KEY must be 64 hex chars (32 bytes).');` (mfa.service.ts:31-33).
impact: A malformed MFA_MASTER_KEY (wrong length / non-hex) passes loadEnv() and only fails when the support/MFA module instantiates. That is still boot-time (DI builds the module at startup) and fail-closed, so impact is limited to a slightly later, less obvious failure point than the other secrets. Noted for consistency, not a vulnerability.
fix: Optional: add the same `/^[0-9a-fA-F]{64}$/` validation in env.ts when reading MFA_MASTER_KEY so all secret validation is centralized and fails at the earliest point.

title: Stale test comment in stripe-retry.job.spec.ts misdescribes the sweep lock (the code is correct)
evidence: The spec mock comment claims "The sweep now claims the controller's `stripe:event:<id>` SETNX lock before dispatch (STRIPE-RETRY-NO-LOCK)", but the actual sweep uses a sweep-private key `const SWEEP_LOCK = (id) => \`stripe:retry-sweep:${id}\`` with a 300s TTL — which is the CORRECT behavior (so it doesn't contend with the controller's 30-day dedup key and can rescue crash-recovery rows). The implementation matches the audit requirement; only the test comment is misleading.
impact: No runtime impact. Documentation drift only — could mislead a future maintainer into 'fixing' the sweep to reuse the controller lock, which would reintroduce the crash-recovery skip the design deliberately avoids.
fix: Update the spec comment to state the sweep uses its own private `stripe:retry-sweep:<id>` lock, distinct from the controller's `stripe:event:<id>` dedup key.

title: Idempotency replay does not re-assert the original HTTP status code (cosmetic; not a correctness bug)
evidence: On a winning claim the interceptor stores only `{ body }` (line 84) and on replay returns `of(parsed.body)` (line 102), letting Nest apply the ROUTE's default status to the replay rather than the original response's status. For these routes all success responses are 200/201 so the replayed status matches; and the same-key/different-body case correctly replays the original result (true idempotency-key semantics, not a body-hash mismatch error) which is acceptable for a trusted librarian client. Noted only because a future route returning a dynamic status would replay the wrong code.
impact: None today — all four circulation routes return a fixed success status, so replays are correct. Latent risk if a variable-status route is later decorated with this interceptor.
fix: Optionally persist and restore the original status code alongside the body on replay; document that the interceptor assumes a fixed success status per route.

title: Verified safe: MARCXML XXE, prototype pollution, MARC binary length-field trust, error-message leakage
evidence: fast-xml-parser 5.8.0 (confirmed in node_modules/.pnpm) is invoked with no processEntities/DTD options (lines 142-149), so external entities and DOCTYPE are not resolved — no XXE on the MARCXML path. Custom-field keys are constrained to /^[a-z][a-z0-9_]{1,49}$/ at import.service.ts:300 and written to a fresh object literal (row-mapper.ts:170), and dynamic-validator uses Object.prototype.hasOwnProperty.call (line 49) — no __proto__/constructor pollution. parseBinaryRecord clamps baseAddress to [24, rec.length] (line 73), clamps fieldEnd to rec.length (lines 87-88), and Node's subarray with start>length safely returns empty — a lying directory length/offset can't read out of bounds or crash. dbIssue (import-engine.ts:85-100) truncates raw DB errors to 300 chars but maps P2002/CHECK/FK to friendly messages; raw Prisma messages can still surface a column/constraint name but not connection strings or file paths. No file-path leakage observed in ParseError messages.
impact: None — these are the vectors the prompt asked to re-verify and they hold up. Documented so the audit trail shows they were actually checked at the code/version level, not assumed.
fix: No change required. Optionally tighten dbIssue's fallback (line 99) to a generic message so a Prisma error string can never leak schema internals to a tenant.
